# Is the 2008 Honda Fit Rear Left Wheel Alignment Not Adjustable?

The short answer to whether the rear-left wheel alignment on a 2008 Honda Fit is unadjustable is yes, but only because of how the vehicle's suspension architecture functions. The mechanic provided an accurate reading based on the physics of the chassis, not a limitation in their ability to tune every single parameter.

On the 2008 Honda Fit (first generation), the rear suspension utilizes a solid axle design paired with Panhard rods and torsion bars. Unlike the independent rear suspension found on many modern sedans or the specific setups in newer Fits that allow for camber adjustment, this platform relies entirely on fixed geometry at the rear differential housing. The alignment specifications dictate a specific Camber value (typically around 0 to -1.5 degrees depending on the spec sheet) and Toe settings. However, there are no threaded bolts, eccentric bushings, or adjustable control arms located behind the rear axle that allow a technician to alter the camber angle independently of the rest of the suspension geometry.

When you look at the alignment report image described in your scenario, you will likely see a "Camber" value listed for the rear-left wheel that falls outside the manufacturer's recommended range, perhaps showing significant negative camber wear or positive camber due to spring sag. On an adjustable setup, a technician would locate the eccentric bolt on the upper control arm or the lower trailing arm and rotate it to shift the camber angle until it hit the spec. On this specific model, those adjustment points simply do not exist for the rear axle. The only variables you can tweak are the Toe-in/Toe-out settings via the tie rods at the knuckle.

This creates a distinct engineering trade-off: you cannot fix the camber issue without altering the vehicle's physical structure or replacing components. If the report indicates that the toe is also out of spec, a standard alignment shop can adjust the tie rods to bring the toe back into the green zone. However, if the primary complaint is tire wear driven by excessive rear camber (often indicated by feathering or rapid wear on the inner or outer edges), you are stuck with the current camber angle unless you change the suspension hardware.

Some enthusiasts attempt to solve this by replacing the rear control arms with aftermarket units that feature built-in eccentric bushings or different mounting points. This is a viable technical solution, but it involves dropping the subframe, removing the fuel tank, and dealing with potentially stiffened spring rates if you aren't careful. It effectively turns a $150 alignment job into a $800 suspension rebuild.

Regarding the question of how to use the car without going through tires yearly: there is no software patch or setting change that will correct this. The relationship between tire load and contact patch is mechanical, not digital. If you continue to run the vehicle with incorrect rear camber, you are essentially forcing the rubber to slide against the asphalt at an angle, generating heat and wearing the tread prematurely.

If the toe is adjustable and within spec while only the camber is bad, you might consider rotating the tires front-to-rear more frequently than usual (e.g., every 4,000 miles instead of 8,000) to even out wear rates across all four corners. However, this is a palliative measure, not a cure. If the camber deviation is severe enough to cause immediate failure of new tires, replacing the rear control arms with adjustable aftermarket units is the only path forward that restores the geometry without modifying the subframe or suspension mounts.
